title: Nrisimhananda Brahmachari
html:
Pradyumna, Whom the Lord Named Nrisimhananda

His earlier name was Pradyumna Brahmachari. He worshipped Lord Nrisimhadeva, and Sri Chaitanya, seeing how devoted he was to his Deity, gave him a new name — Nrisimhananda, “the joy of Nrisimha.” Listing the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, Krishnadasa Kaviraja names him as the thirteenth branch and says of him:

“Pradyumna Brahmachari was a worshipper of Sri Nrisimha, and the Lord gave him the name Nrisimhananda.” (CC, Adi 10.35)

And once more, in the Antya-lila:

“His own name was Pradyumna Brahmachari; it was Gaura, the golden Lord, who named him Nrisimhananda.” (CC, Antya 2.53)

So the original sources call him: Vrindavana Dasa — Pradyumna Brahmachari; Murari Gupta — now Nrisimhananda, now Pradyumna Brahmachari; Kavi Karnapura in his drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” calls him “the famous Sri Nrisimhananda-brahmachari, formerly known as Pradyumna-brahmachari,” says that the Lord Himself gave him the new name for his worship of Nrisimha, and explains the name in two ways: “the joy of Nrisimha” and “he who rejoices in Nrisimha” (act 9). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati writes in the “Anubhashya”: “Pradyumna, or Nrisimha Brahmachari.” Nrisimha was his chosen Deity (ishta-deva); the “Charitamrita” says so plainly: he set out the third offering “for his worshipful Deity, Nrisimha” (Antya 2.61).

Of his worldly life the sources say almost nothing: neither his birthplace, nor his parents, nor the year and day of his appearance or departure. Nor are his days found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. Only Srila Bhaktisiddhanta remarks in the “Anubhashya” that Pradyumna Brahmachari formerly lived in the village of Piyariganj near Kalna.1

The Servant of Nrisimha

Vrindavana Dasa speaks of him twice, and both times of his closeness to Nrisimhadeva. When, in Puri, after the arrival of Svarupa Damodara, the Lord's associates were gathering around Him, he came too:

“Sri Pradyumna Brahmachari was the servant of Lord Nrisimha; Nrisimha Himself was manifest in his body. He came and joined the Lord, understanding that Nrisimha was enjoying the pastimes of kirtana in the form of a sannyasi.” (CB, Antya 3.186–187)

And telling how the devotees of Gauda, led by Advaita, went to Nilachala for the Ratha-yatra, Vrindavana Dasa names him among them:

“Pradyumna Brahmachari also went, with whom Nrisimha Himself speaks face to face.” (CB, Antya 8.12)2

Murari Gupta, too, sees him among Advaita's companions on the way to Puri: “Vakreshvara Pandita and Pradyumna Brahmachari” (Murari Gupta's “Karcha,” 4.17.4). That Nrisimha spoke with him face to face and was manifest in his body is no worldly trance and no possession by an alien power. It is the Lord's mercy to His servant: Nrisimha Himself reveals Himself to one who serves Him with love, and the devotee even then remains “the servant of Nrisimha.” And he recognized his Lord in the sannyasi singing the names of Krishna in Nilachala — recognized that Nrisimha and Sri Chaitanya are one and the same Lord — and stayed with Him.

Year after year he came to Puri with the Bengali devotees. On their first visit Gopinatha Acharya, standing on the palace roof, pointed them out to King Prataparudra by name: “This is Hari Bhatta, this is Sri Nrisimhananda; this is Vasudeva Datta, and this is Shivananda” (CC, Madhya 11.87). In another year Krishnadasa Kaviraja names him in a long list of those who went to Puri, next to Shuklambara Brahmachari (CC, Antya 10.9–11). And Govinda Dasa's “Karcha” mentions Pradyumna Brahmachari among the sannyasis and devotees who gradually gathered around the Lord in Nilachala — together with Shankara Bharati, Paramananda Puri, Damodara Svami and others (3.502).3

The Road of Jewels

After His sannyasa Nityananda cleverly brought the Lord to Shantipura, to Advaita's house, and from there the Lord went to Puri; with Him went Nityananda, Jagadananda, Damodara Pandita and Mukunda Datta. On returning from His journey through South India, He resolved to go to Vrindavana by way of Gauda. In Bengal He stayed in the house of Vidya-vachaspati, Sarvabhauma's brother; then He went to Kuliya, where He showed His grace to Devananda Pandita and forgave Gopala Chapala; and then He reached Ramakeli and met Rupa and Sanatana (CC, Madhya 1.150–153, 166).

When Nrisimhananda heard that the Lord was going to Vrindavana, he began to serve Him in the way he knew — in meditation. Krishnadasa Kaviraja tells it:

“When Nrisimhananda heard that the Lord would go to Vrindavana, he joyfully decorated the road in his mind. From the town of Kuliya he paved the road with jewels and spread over it a bed of flowers with their stems removed. On both sides of the road stood rows of flowering bakula trees, and here and there on either side lay divine ponds. Their bathing steps were set with jewels, and lotuses bloomed in them; many birds chattered, and the water was like nectar. A cool breeze blew, bearing many fragrances. Thus he paved the road as far as Kanai's Natashala.” (CC, Madhya 1.155–159)

Kanai-natashala is a village near Gauda; according to one of the biographies, it lies some two hundred miles north of Calcutta, five miles from Rajmahal, in what is now the Santal Parganas district. Beyond that place the road would not go:

“Beyond that point his mind could not go, nor could he pave any further; the road came to a halt, and Nrisimhananda was astonished. ‘I tell you with certainty — listen, O devotees: this time the Lord will not go to Sri Vrindavana. He will turn back from Kanai's Natashala. You will see it later; I have said this with certainty.’” (CC, Madhya 1.160–162)4

And so it happened. The Lord set out from Kuliya, and thousands of people followed Him (Madhya 1.163); but from Kanai-natashala He turned back to Shantipura, and went to Vrindavana only later. Telling of this return, Krishnadasa Kaviraja again recalls “how Nrisimhananda decorated the road for Him” (Madhya 16.214).

Other original sources also remember this road. Murari Gupta writes that Nrisimhananda, absorbed in thought, paved the way to Madhupuri with gold, silver, coral and gems, spread it with the finest Chinese silks and with flowers without stems, and adorned it with ponds of lotuses and water lilies, with jewelled steps, cygnets and water hens; bringing the road to the “place of dancing,” he enacted there Krishna's forest pastimes, and then, laughing and dancing, announced to the devotees that from there the Lord would turn back. The devotees walked around him and fell prostrate before him, and he lovingly bowed to them in return (Murari Gupta's “Karcha,” 3.17.6–13); and later Murari recalls “the excellent road laid down by Sri Nrisimhananda” (4.25.30). Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” says that the Lord came to Shantipura “along the road adorned by Nrisimha, who knew beforehand of His coming” — with trees full of fruit and flowers and the ground strewn with blossoms (13.37). Lochana Dasa, too, sings of this road in the “Chaitanya-mangala,” but tells of it in his own way.5

This is no daydream and no play of fancy. Service in the mind (manasi-seva) is as real as service with physical articles, and even higher. Rupa Gosvami in the “Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu” speaks of such service: “Some, joyfully serving Hari with offerings made in the mind, attained Him face to face — Him whom speech and mind cannot reach” (1.2.182). One of the biographies recalls here the story of a brahmana of Pratishthanapura who by service in the mind attained the company of Narayana in Vaikuntha.6 And that Nrisimhananda's meditation could go no further than Kanai-natashala was a revelation of the Lord's will: serving in his mind, the devotee learned where the Lord would go — and the prediction came true.

The Lord Appears to Him

Krishnadasa Kaviraja says that Sri Gaura, who descended for the good of all the worlds, delivered souls in three ways:

“To some He granted the sight of Himself in person; in some places He entered a worthy devotee (‘avesha’), and in others He appeared (‘avirbhava’). By being seen in person He delivered almost everyone; and He ‘entered’ the body of Nakula Brahmachari. Before Pradyumna Nrisimhananda He appeared (‘avirbhava’). ‘I shall deliver the people’ — such is the Lord's nature.” (CC, Antya 2.4–6)

The first way is sakshat, when the Lord is present with the devotees in person; the second is avesha, when He enters a devotee with His power, as He entered Nakula Brahmachari; the third is avirbhava, when He reveals Himself where He is not present in person. As the example of the third Kaviraja names Nrisimhananda, already in the Adi-lila:

“His earlier name was Pradyumna Brahmachari; afterwards the Lord gave him the name Nrisimhananda. In him Sri Chaitanya manifested Himself (avirbhava). The Lord has many such wonderful, unearthly ways.” (CC, Adi 10.58–59)

All three kinds of this mercy were tasted by Shivananda Sena (Adi 10.60).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya” on this passage: when the Lord is present in person, the devotees all appear alike — as servants of one kind; but Sriman Mahaprabhu Himself entered Nrisimhananda, and therefore Shivananda Sena and others saw in him the very likeness of Sri Gaurasundara: filled with love for Krishna and performing more wonderful, unearthly deeds than any other devotee. They saw him so not because he himself had become God, but by the power of the Lord who had entered His servant.

And Kavi Karnapura writes in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”:

“The appearance (avirbhava) of Gaurahari was in Nakula Brahmachari; and His entering (avesha) is likewise to be known in the Mishra named Pradyumna.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 73–74)

Literally the verse speaks of Pradyumna Mishra, the Orissan devotee of Puri. But Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” refers it not to the Mishra but to Pradyumna Brahmachari; so too does the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” which calls Nrisimhananda “an avesha of Gaura.”7

Neither avesha nor avirbhava means possession. The Lord does not seize a devotee with an alien power: He who is drawn by love comes Himself to one who loves Him. “He is drawn by prema: that is the Lord's innate nature” (CC, Antya 2.34) — and therefore, Kaviraja continues, Sri Chaitanya constantly manifested Himself in four places: in mother Shachi's household shrine, where Nityananda dances, at Shrivasa's kirtana and in the house of Raghava Pandita (Antya 2.34–35, 79–80). So the Lord delivers even those who cannot come to Him themselves.

The Three Offerings

How the Lord appeared to Nrisimhananda, Krishnadasa Kaviraja tells in the second chapter of the Antya-lila:

“Appearing before Nrisimhananda, He took a meal. Hear of it attentively.” (CC, Antya 2.36)

Once Shrikanta Sena, Shivananda's nephew, came to Puri alone. For two months he lived near the Lord, and then the Lord sent him back to Bengal with a message: this year let no one come — He would come to Gauda in person, to see Advaita and all the devotees; and in the month of Pausha He would be Shivananda's guest, and Jagadananda, who lived with him, would cook for Him (Antya 2.37–43). The devotees rejoiced and stayed at home. Shivananda and Jagadananda made everything ready and throughout Pausha waited for the Lord every day until evening. But the month passed, the Lord did not come, and both grew sorrowful (Antya 2.44–47). The “Charitamrita” does not name the year of these events: it was already in the Antya-lila.

Then Nrisimhananda came to them. Seeing their sorrow, he asked why they grieved, and Shivananda replied: the Lord promised to come — why has He not come? “Hearing this, the brahmachari said, ‘Be content. I shall bring Him on the third day’” (CC, Antya 2.51).8 Both knew his power and his love for the Lord, and believed him without a moment's doubt (Antya 2.52). In Karnapura the story begins differently: Shivananda himself turns to him — “Teacher! The Lord said, ‘I shall come,’ and He has not come” — and he replies, “I myself shall bring Him; wait two days” (act 9).

For two days he remained in meditation, and then he said to Shivananda:

“I have brought the Lord to the village of Panihati. Tomorrow at noon He will come to your house. Bring the provisions for cooking; I shall offer Him bhiksha. Then I shall quickly bring Him here. I tell you this with certainty — have no doubt at all.” (CC, Antya 2.54–56)9

“Brought” does not mean that the devotee commands the Lord, as a yogi might by his powers. The Lord yields to love by His own will, and Nrisimhananda's power is the power of his love. Shivananda brought everything he asked for (Antya 2.57–58).

At dawn Nrisimhananda himself cooked many dishes — soups, vegetable dishes, sweet rice, cakes (pitha) and various delicacies — and divided them into three offerings: for Jagannatha, for Sri Chaitanya and for his own Deity, Nrisimhadeva. Having offered them, he sat outside and became absorbed in meditation (Antya 2.59–61). Karnapura adds that before cooking he bathed and was perfectly pure, and that he offered each plate in its own name, went out and closed his eyes (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” act 9).

“He saw Chaitanya Gosani quickly come and sit down. He ate all three offerings, and nothing was left.” (CC, Antya 2.62)

This was no vision born of the mind: the Lord truly accepted his food, and it became prasada; later, in Puri, the Lord Himself confirmed it. And Nrisimhananda, beside himself with happiness, with tears of bliss in his eyes, cried out:

“Alas, alas! What are You doing? You and Jagannatha are one, so You may eat His offering. But why do You take Nrisimha's offering? I see that today Nrisimha has had to fast. If the master goes without food, how can his servant live?” (CC, Antya 2.63–65)

This “reproach” is a play of love. “Although his heart rejoiced at seeing the Lord eat, outwardly, for Nrisimha's sake, he made some show of sorrow” (Antya 2.66). In Karnapura he weeps aloud, streaming with tears — “in loving anger and with gracious reproach”: “Today, through my fault, Nrisimha has been left hungry!” (act 9). He did not doubt the Lord, nor was he offended with Him. The biographies explain: he knew that Mahaprabhu, Nrisimha and Jagannatha are not different on the highest level, and he spoke so in order to show his fidelity to his chosen Deity.

And Kaviraja discloses the meaning of this pastime:

“Krishna Chaitanya Gosani is Svayam Bhagavan, the Supreme Lord Himself: between Him and Jagannatha and Nrisimha there is no difference at all. Pradyumna had a secret wish to know this, and the Lord showed it to him by eating the offerings.” (CC, Antya 2.67–68)

This is not the impersonal “all gods are one.” Sri Krishna Chaitanya is Bhagavan Himself, the original Lord, and Jagannatha and Nrisimha are His own forms, Vishnu-tattva; by tasting the three offerings at once, the Lord showed Pradyumna that He is not different from all the forms of Vishnu.

Pleased with the skilfully cooked dishes, the Lord went to Panihati (Antya 2.69). Nrisimhananda lamented, “Alas, alas!” Shivananda asked the reason, and he answered:

“He alone has eaten the offerings meant for all three, and Jagannatha and Nrisimha have been left fasting.” (CC, Antya 2.71)

Shivananda began to doubt: had this really happened, or was Nrisimhananda speaking so, overflowing with divine love (Antya 2.72)? Karnapura renders his thought with the words “in a state of avesha” (act 9); here too it is not possession, but the same ecstasy of love. Nrisimhananda asked for provisions once more, and Shivananda brought them; according to Karnapura, it was Shivananda himself who proposed it, and Nrisimhananda was pacified. And he cooked a second time and offered the food to Nrisimhadeva (Antya 2.73–74).

The following year Shivananda, as usual, brought the Bengali devotees to Nilachala.

“One day, in the assembly, the Lord brought up the subject and began to speak of Nrisimhananda's virtues: ‘Last year, in Pausha, he fed Me. Never have I eaten such sweets and vegetable dishes.’ Hearing this, the devotees were filled with wonder, and then conviction was born in Shivananda's mind.” (CC, Antya 2.76–78)

In Karnapura the Lord says that last Pausha He accepted alms from Nrisimhananda and came to know how skilfully he cooks.

Significance

When and where Nrisimhananda left this world the original sources do not say; the day of his departure, like the day of his appearance, is not in our Vaishnava calendar. Only Lochana Dasa writes that, without finishing the road in his mind, he attained Vaikuntha; but the “Charitamrita” shows him in this world after that as well (see note 5).

Krishnadasa Kaviraja counts him among the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, and the Lord Himself appeared to him and tasted his cooking. His life is a story of the love that draws the Lord. Serving in his mind, he paved a road of jewels for the Lord, and by where it ended learned His will. Having promised the sorrowing devotees to bring the Lord to them, he kept his word, and the Lord Himself later praised his meal before everyone. And by the three offerings the Lord revealed to him, and to all who hear this story, that Sri Krishna Chaitanya, Bhagavan Himself, is not different from Jagannatha and Nrisimha; while Nrisimhananda's “complaint” is a lesson in fidelity to one's chosen Deity.

One of the biographies warns: one who considers the Lord's body a product of material nature is deceived by the illusory energy; he mocks such accounts as fables and passes this off as learning; bereft of faith in the Lord, he is a pauper, deprived of all that is truly valuable, and gains only births and deaths. But for one who has faith, the story of Nrisimhananda bears witness that the Lord still comes to those who serve Him with love.

Notes

  1. According to Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura's “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya,” it was Nakula Brahmachari who lived in Piyariganj (in the district of Ambua, or Ambika, near Kalna); perhaps the two brahmacharis have been confused here.
  2. The “Anubhashya” and one of the biographies place this line in the ninth chapter of the Antya-khanda of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”; in our edition it is Antya 8.12 — evidently the chapters are divided differently in different editions. Another biography cites the first passage (Antya 3.186–187) as verses of the “Charitamrita,” and the second with a different number (Antya 8.92). Some references to the “Charitamrita” in the first of them are also inexact: verses Antya 2.53 and 2.76 are assigned there to the Adi-lila.
  3. The authenticity of Govinda Dasa's “Karcha” is disputed.
  4. According to one of the biographies, the meditation broke off when the Lord reached Kanai-natashala, and only then did Nrisimhananda understand that He would go no further. According to the “Charitamrita,” he told the devotees so beforehand (Madhya 1.161–162); we follow it.
  5. In Lochana Dasa (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Shesha-khanda, ch. 2, vv. 18–24) Nrisimhananda is a sannyasi, and he builds the road in his mind from Purushottama to Mathura, of pearls, coral, gold and rubies, so that Gora might walk on it; but having brought it only as far as Kanai's Natashala, he attains Vaikuntha, and the Lord, fulfilling his heart's wish, turns back from Kanai's Natashala and explains this to Paramananda Puri. According to the “Charitamrita,” Nrisimhananda is a brahmachari, the road begins at Kuliya, and he himself foretells the Lord's return to the devotees, and later, in the Antya-lila, brings the Lord to Shivananda and goes to Puri; so Lochana perhaps confuses him with one of his sannyasi namesakes (Nrisimha Puri, Narasimha Tirtha). In Murari Gupta the road runs “from the Kshetra” (usually the name of Puri, though the Lord is already in Bengal at this time). We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  6. The verse number (Purva-vibhaga 2.182) is correct; the translation of the verse is ours. The story of the brahmana of Pratishthanapura itself (after the “Brahma-vaivarta Purana”: he cooked sweet rice for the Lord in his mind, burnt his fingers, and the Lord of Vaikuntha took him to Himself) is told not in Rupa Gosvami's verse but in Srila Vishvanatha Chakravarti's commentary on it.
  7. The “Charitamrita” itself assigns the kinds of mercy the other way round: entering (avesha) in Nakula, appearing (avirbhava) before Nrisimhananda (Adi 10.57–59; Antya 2.4–6). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on Adi 10.35 cites the verse GGD 74 under Pradyumna Brahmachari, and on Adi 10.57 speaks of Mahaprabhu's entering into Nrisimhananda; on Adi 10.56 he names entering “in Nakula or Pradyumna Brahmachari,” and then, following the “Gaura-ganoddesha,” appearance and entering in Nakula Brahmachari and Pradyumna Mishra. In the narrative we follow the words of the “Charitamrita.”
  8. One of the biographies says “within three days,” and both say that Pausha had “almost ended”; according to the “Charitamrita” — “on the third day,” when the month had already passed (Antya 2.47, 2.51).
  9. That Shivananda's house was in Kumarahatta is stated by the “Anubhashya” on Adi 10.35 (the Lord came there from Raghava's house in Panihati) and by the biographies. In the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” Nrisimhananda says, “The Lord has been brought to Raghava's house,” and the events themselves are placed in the year when Ramananda Raya persuaded the Lord to remain in Puri and He did not go to Gauda (act 9). We follow the “Charitamrita.”
